national.summary: Police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel.
national.body: Japanese prosecutors have indicted a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering a woman on Okinawa, a court spokesman told AFP on Monday, in a case that prompted public outrage. The alleged killing of the 39-year-old Japanese woman caused Japan's premier to slam the "heinous crime" and reignited controversy over the heavy U.S. military presence on the southern island. "The case was indicted on October 25," said the spokesman for the court in Naha, confirming media reports that the suspect had been indicted on charges of murder and robbery.Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha. The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that, according to the indictment document, the suspect allegedly strangled the woman from Naha in a hotel with a telephone cord on October 3. He is also accused of stealing a backpack containing the woman's wallet and other belongings, the newspaper said. The Marine denied the allegations at the time of his arrest but has now made statements that imply some involvement in the case, the Yomiuri and other media said, citing investigative sources.Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions in the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops. national.title: Woman, 93, outwits scammer, helps get him arrested, police say
national.summary: A 93-year-old woman in western Japan outsmarted a suspected scammer by pretending to fall for the scheme and helping police arrest him at her home, an officer said.
national.body: A 93-year-old woman in western Japan outsmarted a suspected scammer by pretending to fall for the scheme and helping police arrest him at her home, a police official told AFP on Monday. Japan has the second-oldest population in the world after Monaco, and senior citizens are often targeted by fraudsters, who last year collectively stole around 325.7 billion yen ($2.0 billion) from their victims. The woman, who lives in the Shiga region, received telephone calls from Wednesday through Thursday last week from a man who claimed to be a police officer. The caller falsely informed her that her bank account had experienced an unauthorized withdrawal. The woman was told to give her ATM card to a man, posing as a police officer, who would visit her so authorities could verify her account. Suspecting a scam, the woman consulted her son and the police as she waited for the man to visit her house. "The person's family reached out to the police on Wednesday evening, and we were able to have officers at her house" before the scammer arrived on Thursday, a local police official told AFP on the customary condition of anonymity. When a 47-year-old man appeared at her doorstep, waiting officers arrested him on the spot, the police official said. "The person (the woman) is someone in good health and highly articulate," the official said, while urging other elderly residents to consult family members when they suspect fraud.

national.title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
national.summary: President Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States.
national.body:
President Donald Trump departs after speaking during a campaign rally at McMorran Place Sports and Entertainment Center, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Mich. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

PORT HURON, Mich. — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.

Elections Republicans are spending millions and still may not win districts drawn to favor them Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.

El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.

"The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.

Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.

Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."

national.title: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
national.summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
national.body:
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded late on Sunday, citing preliminary figures that gave the students 2.2 million votes and his party 1.72 million.

The students were on course to win 52.9% of the vote, according to a later projection by independent pollsters CeSID, with the highest turnout for years of 69.34%.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."

national.title: Loggers say Roadless Rule repeal won't solve their biggest challenges
national.summary: President Trump is planning to open up some of the nation's last pristine forests to road building and timber companies. But those who work in the woods say it won't do enough to revive the industry.
national.body:
Logs from a salvage timber sale after a recent wildfire in the Willamette National Forest in Oregon. Kirk Siegler hide caption

EUGENE, Ore. - President Trump is widely expected to soon open up some 44 million acres of the country's last pristine national forests in a move he says will bring timber jobs back to struggling small towns and help prevent wildfires in overgrown lands.

Trump signaled the move with executive actions last year aimed at dramatically boosting timber sales on U.S. Forest Service land and reversing the agency's 25-year-old Roadless Rule, which blocked most new logging on undeveloped national forestlands.

Today with the formal repeal of the Roadless Rule rule expected early next year, the picture on the ground in timber country looks messier. Those who make a living in the forests say the problems are much bigger than access to more trees.

"I'm not saying these EOs [Executive Orders] are useless, they set the tone," says Sean Smith, CEO of the family owned Starfire Lumber in Cottage Grove, Ore.

Smith, standing in a bustling lumber yard with the sawmill cranking behind four story high stacks of freshly cut timber, says the industry has more pressing challenges now, starting with the record high price of diesel fuel. Economists largely blame that on Trump's war with Iran. And then there's inflation, which is driving up the costs of just about everything.

"Steel, you know, we have to buy sawblades, we have to buy ball bearings," Smith says. "We have to buy a million different parts to keep this mouse trap going."

So repealing the Roadless Rule - which has largely banned new road building and logging projects on some 44 million acres of pristine national forests since 2001 - is lower on the priority list.

national.title: How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
national.summary: Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions.
national.body:
A satellite image provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows Hurricane Isaias approaching the Gulf Coast of Alabama and Florida on Friday, Oct. 9 2026. NOAA/NOAA hide caption

Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.

When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.

Climate The Pacific is churning with hurricanes. The Atlantic is quiet. Blame El Niño In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.

But Google DeepMind's artificial intelligence model called it right out of the gate: the hurricane was going to hit the western Florida Panhandle.

"Google DeepMind, in particular, has really proven itself the last few years as the gold standard model," says Michael Lowry, a longtime meteorologist and hurricane expert in Miami, who has previously advised both the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

"That model has been, by far and away, the best performing computer model that we've ever seen. Period."

The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating the Google DeepMind model into its official forecasts last year.

national.title: Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
national.summary: What makes special education teaching jobs so hard to fill? NPR set out to find some answers by talking to more than a dozen teachers who do this work every day.
national.body:
Top row (from left): Danalyn Garcia of Chicago Public Schools, Lucie Lane of Shawnee Mission School District in Kansas, Jeff Carroll of Newport News Public Schools in Virginia and Kaori Anderson-Walker of Boys' Latin of Philadelphia Charter School. Bottom row (from left): Paul Stone of Mt. Diablo Unified School District in California, Diana Swanson of Vail School District in Arizona, Kathleen Tejeda of Alvord Unified School District in California and Emily Ellis of Lexington School District Two in South Carolina. LA Johnson/NPR hide caption

One of Kathleen Tejeda's students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person.

By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school.

Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find.

There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states , according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It's now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students.

While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn't new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent?

Let's start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don't want to do the job. "That is not the case," said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. "That has not borne out in our research at all."

What Bettini's research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don't get paid enough to do this essential work.

national.title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo
national.summary: Uganda will also not allow most travellers who have been in DR Congo to transit through the country.
national.body:
Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of Ebola virus.

More than 4,800 people have died in DR Congo since May - the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease - and has since spread to several other countries.

Uganda's restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola, in Kenya and Nigeria.

The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged.

Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda.

It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".

Uganda has also "intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints", it added.

Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to "intense public health measures".

national.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in Party
national.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.
national.body:
China correspondent Published 3 hours ago A major political gathering is underway in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.

The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.

The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.

The normally annual Plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.

They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.

There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.

The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.

Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.

national.title: Jordan says 3 arrested in deadly attack on Greek Orthodox church
national.summary: Jordan says its security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.
national.body: Amman, Jordan — Jordanian security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects were arrested following a dawn shootout and that all three were wounded. No members of the security forces were injured in the dawn operation in Karak governorate, south of Jordan's capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. The attack on the Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.There was still no claim of responsibility, and no armed group has been accused of the attack. Jordan's Interior Minister, Mazen Al-Faraya, identified the three men as those responsible for the attack. "The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," he said in a phone interview with state TV Al-Mamlaka. "They put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."He added that there "are three individuals involved; they were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."The directorate said, "Terrorism has no place among us," and that the three had met their "just fate," according to the Reuters news agency. The directorate didn't name the suspects or point to any possible links to any Islamist militant groups, Reuters added. King Abdullah II directed authorities to respond with "an iron fist" against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

national.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
national.summary: Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme.
national.body:
Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.

A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram , external said he had died "suddenly".

Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.

Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.

"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said , external . "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."

He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.

He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.

Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.

A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram , external said he had died "suddenly".

Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.

Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.

"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said , external . "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."

He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.

He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.

national.body: Eric Bauza, the Emmy-winning actor who voiced iconic "Looney Tunes" characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, according to his manager. He was 46."Eric was a unique and versatile voice actor who was loved by everyone he knew and worked with," said Judy Coppage, Bauza's manager. "His sudden passing is a shock to all of us, and he will be deeply missed. It's a profound loss for his family, the animation industry and his fans."Bauza, who was born in Canada, died from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. His family posted a brief statement on his Instagram page, adding that more details would come later.Bauza had more than 400 acting credits listed on his IMDb page. In addition to voicing Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, Bauza is credited with voicing other "Looney Tunes" characters such as Porky Pig, PepÃ© Le Pew, Marvin the Martian, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety Bird and Road Runner. He also voiced characters in the most recent "Space Jam" film, alongside LeBron James. Beyond "Looney Tunes," Bauza was known for his voice work on shows such as "Avatar: The Last Airbender," "Puss in Boots," "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles," "Woody Woodpecker," "Bob's Burgers" and "Teen Titans Go!"Bauza won Children's and Family Emmy Awards in 2022, 2023 and 2025 and was nominated in 2026. He was also nominated for five Daytime Emmy Awards from 2016 to 2021. He joined CBS LA in August to discuss his latest film and the newest "Looney Tunes" installment, "Coyote vs. Acme." "All of my work is based off of the original voiceover artist, the great Mel Blanc; he was the original. I like to call him the blueprint of these characters," Bauza said. "They're not just voices; these are personalities that we've been familiar with now for 90 years â it's like your oldest family members. national.title: Lula wins 4th term as Brazil's president, but Bolsonaro rejects results
national.summary: With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon-to-be 81-year-old Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva held an insurmountable lead, but Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the results.
national.body: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of Mr. Trump and keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America, where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Mr. Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders. It also means the nation with Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Mr. Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs he imposed. The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out of the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with first lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out in the first round.A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with first lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.I

national.title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
national.summary: Machado had left the country just a month before the US government seized Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
national.body:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.

"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.

In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.

The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.

Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.

She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.

She was photographed smiling as she leaned out of the sunroof of a car as she entered Caracas late on Sunday night.

"Night of reunion in our Caracas. For the reunion of each family, for the Freedom of each political prisoner, for the Freedom of Venezuela," she wrote on X.

national.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
national.summary: Andre McKechnie, who murdered a property developer, argued it was his right to enjoy Australian culture.
national.body:
A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.

Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".

Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.

And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.

McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.

During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.

The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.

national.title: India's cartoonists built an audience online - now their posts are being restricted
national.summary: Indian cartoonists say online restrictions are making satire harder, but they aren't giving up.
national.body:
For the second time in three weeks, Indian cartoonist Satish Acharya found himself effectively invisible on Instagram in his own country.

The 55-year-old discovered on Tuesday that his account had once again been briefly blocked in India, allegedly with no explanation from the platform.

Just a few weeks ago, another cartoonist, Manjul, had found that Instagram had restricted a post criticising India's election commission over its controversial revision of voter rolls. His profile remained accessible.

The cases have raised concerns about the use of legal orders to restrict political satire in India, with cartoonists saying they are often given little explanation for why their work has been blocked.

Acharaya's account was first restricted from 28 September to 6 October, when users in India could neither find his profile through search nor access it through a web link.

Anyone trying to access his profile saw a message saying it was unavailable under India's Information Technology Rules.

The rules allow authorities and courts to order social media platforms to remove or restrict content.

The government says they help tackle unlawful material, but artists and free-speech advocates warn they can stifle India's rich tradition of political satire.

national.summary: Brazil's 80-year-old left-wing leader President Lula defeats Flávio Bolsonaro in a bitterly contested runoff.
national.body:
Supporters of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva cheer as the results of Brazil's presidential runoff election are announced in São Paulo on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Natacha Pisarenko/AP hide caption

BRASILIA, Brazil — In a stunning political comeback, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been elected president of Brazil, according to official results from Sunday's runoff election, with more than 96% of the votes counted.

Lula secured more than 51% of the vote, defeating Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who received more than 48%.

The result marks a historic moment in Brazil's democratic era. Since democracy was restored in 1989, no candidate who failed to win the first round of voting has gone on to win the presidency in the second round.

The victory also adds another chapter to Lula's long political career, securing him a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term. Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, will be among the oldest sitting leaders in the Americas, alongside President Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, both 80.

In a speech to ecstatic supporters in São Paulo, Lula said the election was a "defeat of denialism. A defeat of lies."

"I want to thank the Brazilian people for this generosity they have shown me for so long, to thank the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy, and the elders who went to vote," Lula told the crowd.

national.summary: The shooting happened hours after Florida A&M University's homecoming game in Tallahassee.
national.body: At least 12 people were injured, including six children, in a shooting Saturday near a football stadium in Tallahassee on homecoming weekend for Florida A&M University, authorities said. Eleven people suffered gunshot wounds.Tallahassee police said in a statement Sunday that six of the shooting victims remained hospitalized, and five had been discharged. One of those still hospitalized was being treated for critical injuries.The department previously said at least three people sustained serious injuries in the shooting, while nine others are reported to be in stable condition.The preliminary investigation indicates that a fight broke out before the shooting, according to police. It followed a football game in a crowded area.The Tallahassee Police Department said Sunday that no arrests have been made, but investigators are working to identify those responsible. The department has established a dedicated tip line for people to submit information and a link for people to upload photos and video."We know there are people who saw something, heard something or may have video that could help us piece together exactly what happened," Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said. national.title: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
national.summary: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
national.body:
Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map , external , a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.

El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".

local.title: Hyatt awaits $16M overhaul as other hotels face uncertain future
local.summary: The Riverside and former Wyndham once accounted for nearly half of all downtown hotel rooms. Now one has been ransacked, and the other is wrapped in corrugated steel.
local.body:
A $16 million renovation meant to elevate the downtown Hyatt Regency to a top-flight, full-service hotel will begin "as soon as possible," officials say.

"Our goal is to make it shine again, you know?" said Hyatt general manager Jay Rettberg. "Be that exclamation point."

In a downtown looking to regain its pre-pandemic momentum, the project is a bright spot. The Hyatt has been a critical piece of local travel and tourism. Now it is an anchor in a hotel scene otherwise in flux. It is the largest hotel in the Center City since the Rochester Riverside closed in 2020. The Wyndham was the next largest until it, too, shut down this summer.

"For a city of our size with a population of our size, you know we're short about 1,000 hotel rooms from what we would ideally have," Deputy Mayor Michael Burns said. "And so, the rooms at the Hyatt are critical — as are the rooms over at the former Wyndham Hotel."

The Riverside and former Wyndham accounted for nearly half, almost 700, of all downtown hotel rooms. A lack of hotel capacity, made worse by the closures, has cost the city nearly $50 million in lost meeting business since 2022, according to VisitRochester estimates. And the buildings have become a blight in the heart of downtown — one ransacked , the other wrapped in corrugated steel to head off a similar plight.

local.title: New hires at Lollypop Farm signal the return of vital services for pets and local rescues
local.summary: Staffing shortages this summer temporarily halted spay/neuter surgeries. Three full-time veterinarians were recently hired following a national search.
local.body:
A veterinarian shortage in the U.S. has for years presented challenges to pet owners and rescue groups seeking care for their companion animals.

Even the Rochester region's largest animal welfare organization is not immune to its effects.

In June, Lollypop Farm, the Humane Society of Greater Rochester, temporarily paused spay/neuter surgeries for pets in the care of community rescue organizations due to staff shortages.

This week, Lollypop announced the recent hiring of three veterinarians to close that gap.

"We were recruiting nationally. We did have a search firm helping us out, but ultimately we succeeded most with people who were familiar with the area and had a true passion for shelter medicine," said vice president and COO Adrienne McHargue.

Now, with a total of four full-time staff veterinarians, part-time medical director, and 10 veterinary technicians, as well as the recent addition of veterinarians who helped on a per diem basis during the summer, Lollypop hopes to provide the same level of community service it did in 2024. McHargue said that is when they began losing veterinarians through relocation and discovered it was challenging to find replacements.

As the organization grows its capacity to provide veterinary care, it will be reopening its S.N.I.P program in November. The program allows income eligible pet owners to apply for spay/neuter services for their pets at a reduced cost. Lollypop also expects to improve access to veterinary services for partner rescue organizations in the community, including vaccination clinics, wellness exams, and sterilization surgeries.

A new mobile veterinary clinic is expected to launch in the near future, bringing wellness services directly to underserved communities where transportation may be a barrier for pet owners.

local.title: Both parties see opportunities to make gains in NY Senate
local.summary: Republicans are trying to reduce Democrats’ 41-22 state Senate majority while Democrats are trying to grow it.
local.body:
Early voting has begun for this year’s general election, and every seat in the New York state Legislature is on the ballot.

In the state Senate, Republicans are trying to reduce Democrats’ 41-22 majority while Democrats are trying to grow it.

One race where Democrats see opportunity is the 43rd district, which covers Rensselaer County and parts of Albany and Washington counties. The seat has been long held by Republicans, including former Senate Majority Leader Joe Bruno, but the latest redistricting gives Democrats and unaffiliated voters a registration edge.

Enter Devin Lander , state historian and first-time candidate, who is vying to unseat the district’s incumbent Republican Sen. Jake Ashby .

“I think it's very important symbolically,” Lander said, though noting that the district has changed. “The enrollments are different now. People's expectations are different now. And I think, you know, people are … ready for new leadership.”

“It's a purple district,” Ashby said. "And I think that I represent that, and I have very well ... during my time in the Assembly, and also in the Senate."

Ashby served one term in the Assembly before being elected to the Senate in 2022.

There also are contested seats on Long Island, as well as in the Hudson Valley, the Capital Region and Central New York. Both parties are trying to reach voters contending with the rising cost of living and high energy bills.

local.body:
The reaction was swift earlier this year when the Salamanca City Central School District proposed using a Realbotix educational robot and digital avatar designed to support teaching and learning in its high school STEAM program.

That project was quickly shelved after widespread criticism, but a state lawmaker wants to go a step further by implementing grade-based limits on students' access to internet-enabled devices. Assemblywoman Sarahana Shrestha, D-Kingston, recently introduced the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use Of Screens (FOCUS) Act. The bill (A.11669) would phase in grade-based limits on pupils’ access to Internet-enabled devices and limit the use of social media, gaming, direct messaging, and other apps Shrestha said serve little to no instructional purpose. The legislation would constitute a major change for schools in the state. The earliest it could be discussed is the next state legislative session starting in January.

"Known as the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens (FOCUS) Act, this bill aligns with the precedent set by New York’s 2025 bell-to-bell ban for students’ personal devices, which put an end to the havoc that smartphones were wreaking in classrooms through their ability to addict, distract, and impair the mental health of student users," Shrestha wrote in her legislative justification. "The FOCUS Act builds upon this framework by recognizing that it makes little sense for the State of New York to go through the trouble of limiting personal devices if we are then going to bring them right back in the form of school-issued devices."

For early childhood and elementary school pupils in pre-kindergarten through fifth grades, Shrestha proposes students generally be prohibited from accessing screens and instead complete assignments via pencil and paper wherever feasible. For middle school students in sixth through eighth grades, students will access screens via a computer cart or lab model wherein devices are rotated amongst students in a classroom. High school students would access screens as part of a cart model or on a one-to-one basis with caregiver opt in,

Shrestha also proposes creating a right to analog learning, meaning schools and teachers would prioritize in-class and homework assignments that allow students to complete them in a screen-free manner wherever feasible. Parents and students would additionally be able to opt out of screens where a reasonable non-digital alternative to completing an assignment exists, and schools would be prohibited from retaliating against pupils who exercise this right, The opt-out provision would not apply to assignments where use of the technology is inherent to the learning objective of the assignment, such as assignments undertaken pursuant to the state Education Department's computer science and digital fluency standards.

SAINT-DENIS, France (AP) -- Aaron Rodgers threw one touchdown pass and Chris Boswell kicked three field goals in Pittsburgh’s 16-10 win over the New Orleans Saints on Sunday in the NFL’s first regular-season game in France.

Jaylen Warren rushed for 101 yards and Rodgers completed 19 of 30 passes for 212 yards and scrambled for a key first down late in fourth quarter as the Steelers (5-2) won their third straight game.

Linebacker Payton Wilson had a red zone interception of Tyler Shough in the third quarter and the Saints (2-5) couldn’t recover. New Orleans rushed for just 18 yards.

With the Saints threatening on their opening drive of the second half, Wilson stepped in front of a short pass intended for Chris Olave. The Steelers got in field-goal position and Boswell was good from 39 yards for a 16-10 lead.

CHARLOTTE, N.C. (AP) -- Bucky Irving ran for 106 yards and two touchdowns, and Tampa Bay forced four turnovers as the Buccaneers hammered Carolina in Baker Mayfield’s return.

Mayfield, who missed the previous three games with a dislocated right thumb, attempted just 11 passes and threw for 64 yards while wearing a protective glove on his right hand. That was more than enough for him to improve to 7-1 against the Panthers, including 6-1 since joining the Bucs (2-5).

Mayfield didn’t need to do much because Tampa Bay’s run game, defense and special teams dominated. The Bucs had 258 yards on the ground, with Sean Tucker adding a 46-yard touchdown run to put Tampa Bay up by 37.

Carolina’s Bryce Young turned the ball over three times. Al-Quadin Muhammad had a strip-sack of Young that Calijah Kancey returned 32 yards for a touchdown.

Survivors include a daughter Suzanne (Larry) Near, a son Stephen Prince, and a sister Dorothy Merrill. Also surviving are one granddaughter; Courtney (Wayne) Kelsey, Jr., two great granddaughters; Violet Near-Watkins & Jade Kelsey, several step grandchildren, great grandchildren, nieces, nephews & cousins. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, a new federal Education Freedom Tax Credit provides up to $1,700 per individual (up to $3,400 for married couples filing jointly) for qualified cash contributions to a Scholarship Granting Organization. Yet as with most bills passed out of our Congress, there are regulations and deadlines.

On Oct. 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service released proposed regulations for the credit’s 2027 launch, making the new credit accessible to families and providing administrative guidance for taxpayers, states and SGOs while protecting scholarship funds from fraud and abuse.

SGOs can use contributions from individuals to provide scholarships to students for a range of education-related expenses incurred in connection with a K-12 public, private (including religious) or charter school. This can include tuition for students to attend a school of choice, tutoring for students attending a public school, special education services for students with disabilities, books, supplies and extended day programs.

Why is not this great education freedom opportunity in the headlines during such a consequential midterms election year?

Students from a household whose prior-year income is up to 300% of the area’s median gross income, adjusted for family size, may qualify for a scholarship through the Education Freedom Tax Credit. Our Treasury Department estimates that about 95% of American children live in households that may qualify for such a scholarship.

One challenge for parents in certain states to access these great benefits is that due to an absurd interpretation of U.S. Senate rules by the Senate parliamentarian, senators inserted a state “opt-in” condition for taxpayers in those states to claim the federal credit for contributions to SGOs in their home state.

Yet Treasury reports that as of Sept. 14, 2026, only 30 states have elected to identify SGOs in their state that will be eligible to receive contributions from individuals utilizing the Education Freedom Tax Credit.

SOUTH DAYTON -- Demonstrating that no member of their school family fights alone, 27 students and staff members at Pine Valley Jr/Sr High School gathered in the school gymnasium for an emotional show of support: shaving their heads and cutting their hair in solidarity with Stephanie West, a beloved teacher aide who runs the 7-12 Mandatory Guided Study and In-School Suspension Room, currently undergoing treatment for breast cancer.

The movement began when a group of senior boys decided to shave their heads in solidarity with West following her diagnosis late last school year. Rooted in the district’s core value of “showing up” – demonstrating unity and supporting one another through every challenge – this gesture quickly gained momentum. Classmates and staff joined in to turn the idea into a moving surprise rally for West, filling the gym bleachers, bedecked in pink, greeting her with homemade signs of support and thunderous applause.

With fight songs blaring over the gymnasium speakers, 27 participants took turns in the barber chair as volunteers Kelly Ebel and Chantel Powenski generously donated their time and expertise to shave and cut hair, sending a resounding message of love as Mrs. West continues her treatment.

“(She) is a remarkable individual who makes connections with all the students she encounters. We could not function as a school without her,” said Kourtney Almeida, Pine Valley Jr/Sr High School Principal.

“Several of our students volunteered to shave their heads in honor of Mrs. West. Their actions represent courage, kindness, compassion, and the power of standing beside someone when they need us most,” Almeida added. “Mrs. West, we want you to know that you are not fighting alone. You have an entire school community standing behind you, cheering you on, and supporting you every step of the way. To our students who shaved their heads, thank you for showing what it truly means to be part of the Panther family.”

The event coincides with Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reinforcing the district's core campaign, #PVShowsUp.

local.title: West Side resident describes horrifying crash-prone intersection
local.summary: David Pinero has captured six car accidents on the corner of Barton and West Ferry Streets through his home security camera.
local.body: David Pinero has captured six car accidents on the corner of Barton and West Ferry Streets through his home security camera. He has lived at that intersection for three years, but over the past two, he has seen an increase in crashes with one landing on his bushes.Pinero and his landlord both live at the corner house and told 7 news that they have filed a 311 with the City of Buffalo in hopes that new signs are put up at the intersection because they said that children live there and are worried about a tragedy that could be prevented."They're out of control and they're missiles," said Pinero. "You have kids going to school every day. They go up this street, they go up that street, they play in this yard in the summer. So, at any time, any of these cars that consistently either land up here or land over there are you're looking at a very terrible outcome, worst-case scenario, if that ever happens when they're out."The intersection is not a four-way stop, so Pinero said he believes the accidents are caused by the driver going down Barton Street, is making the assumption that West Ferry also has stop signs."So most of them stop. And then when they're satisfied that they see a car coming and it too will stop, they move forward, and that's a miscalculation. That's when you get your impacts," Pinero tells 7 News.7 News reached out to the city to see if they have taken Pinero's complaint. A spokesperson told us in a statement that an inspector will come out within the next week. The city also said the timing of the process is based on resource availability, but it's hoping to get a four-way stop in abut a month.

entertainment.title: ‘All About the Money’ Doc Director Explains How She Updated Her Doc on Fergie Chambers – and Her Concerns About That U.S. Extradition Request
entertainment.summary: Irish director Sinéad O’Shea is gearing up for much debate as the film comes into U.K. and Irish cinemas on Oct. 30 after its BFI London Film Festival run and before screening at DOC NYC in November.
entertainment.body:
The works of Irish documentary director Sinéad O’Shea tend to turn heads and cause debate. Her latest film, All About the Money , which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival before recently screening at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF), is no different.

Exploring themes of money, power and revolution, the doc follows James Cox Chambers, who goes by Fergie Chambers, a member of the family whose holdings include Cox Enterprises, as he travels the world in pursuit of making a difference. No stranger to controversy, the doc shows him discussing what drives him and the world. Related Stories Business Ted Sarandos Swoops Into Seoul as Netflix Celebrates 10 Years in Korea TV A Peek Into 'SNL UK': Strict Security, Giddy Cynthia Erivo and Sometimes More a Party Than a TV Set

The film also goes into his pro-Palestine and anti-Israel activism, which has landed him in the headlines in recent months. In July, Spanish authorities arrested Chambers; he is being held in Madrid. The Guardian then reported that FBI agents raided his Ibiza, Spain, vacation rental. The U.S. has made an extradition request, citing Chambers’ alleged financial support of Hamas and other charges.

O’Shea, who wrote and directed the doc, produced by Claire McCabe, Harry Vaughn, Katie Holly, and Sigrid Dyekjær, with SOS Productions and Real Lava co-producing, caught up with THR about the recent activity surrounding the man at the center of her doc, which will screen in U.K. and Ireland cinemas from Oct. 30 after a recent run at the BFI London Film Festival (LFF).

“The case is sealed, but his lawyers have told me that [one of the] accusations is that he transferred money from the U.S. and used it to finance Hamas,” O’Shea says. As she shows in the film, Chambers moved to Tunisia where he bought a soccer club after his pro-Palestine activism led to arrests following what critics called an ill-conceived protest of an Israeli defense contractor. “He went to Tunisia and invested in a [soccer] club,” says the filmmaker about what she has documented. “So it’s a really strange, but very serious, accusation against him that that money was used for Hamas. It just doesn’t really make any sense to me. … I think … they will have an extensive paper trail of how that money worked.”

His legal team has said that Chambers has strictly donated to lawful Gaza and Palestine humanitarian and philanthropic aid projects, and O’Shea believes them.

entertainment.title: Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71
entertainment.summary: The Scottish-born executive worked with Radiohead, My Morning Jacket and St. Vincent across stints at Warner/Chappell, Chrysalis and his own indie publisher.
entertainment.body:
Kenny MacPherson , the longtime music publishing executive who co-founded independent publisher Big Deal Music , died Oct. 23 in Los Angeles. He was 71. No cause of death was given. Explore My Morning Jacket OutKast Radiohead See latest videos, charts and news

Over nearly four decades, MacPherson became one of the most recognizable figures in music publishing , known for a sharp ear for left-of-center talent and a loyalty to the songwriters he signed. “Kenny was one of a kind,” Supertramp bassist Dougie Thomson, a friend of 50 years, told HITS Daily Double . Former Big Deal partner Jamie Cerreta, now president of Peermusic U.S. and Canada, said MacPherson “was beloved by the songwriters he fought so hard for.” Related Diddy Moved From New Jersey Prison to Similar Facility in Pennsylvania Weezer to Receive Legend of Live Award at 2026 Billboard Live Music Summit Hilary Duff to Receive Outstanding Pop Tour of the Year Award at 2026 Billboard Live Music Summit

Born in Largs, Scotland, MacPherson got his start in live music in Glasgow, eventually managing concerts at the city’s Apollo Theatre. There he met comedian Billy Connolly, whom he went on to tour-manage, and it was in the London offices of Connolly’s publishers that he got the advice that set his course. “You know, Kenny, if you want to be in the music business, get into publishing — it’s a gentleman’s game,” publisher Bill Martin told him, as MacPherson recalled in a 2019 interview with Billboard .

He moved to the U.S. in the late 1970s and early ’80s, working with the Manhattan Transfer and then Supertramp’s management company, where he helped launch a publishing arm. In 1989 he joined Warner/Chappell to run its New York office, and over 13 years there he signed or developed acts including Radiohead , Underworld, Paul Westerberg, the Afghan Whigs and the Blue Nile.

He then took over Chrysalis Music’s North American division, where he and his team signed OutKast , My Morning Jacket , Ray LaMontagne , TV on the Radio, the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Beach House, St. Vincent and Thom Yorke , along with producers including Ethan Johns and Dave Sitek. He led the division until BMG acquired Chrysalis in 2010.

In 2012, MacPherson co-founded Big Deal Music with longtime colleagues Dave Ayers and Jamie Cerreta. “I wanted to build a place that was culturally significant and great for people to work, where manners, courtesy and high touch are important,” he told Billboard in 2019. With offices in Los Angeles, New York and Nashville, the company reunited him with past signings like LaMontagne, My Morning Jacket and St. Vincent while adding Blake Mills, Weyes Blood, Kamasi Washington, Sharon Van Etten, Sylvan Esso, Sleater-Kinney and hitmaking writers Teddy Geiger, Julian Bunetta and John Ryan. It regularly ranked among the top 10 U.S. publishers by market share, and the Association of Independent Music Publishers named it indie publisher of the year in 2017.

entertainment.body:
President Donald Trump is once again criticizing Bill Maher , host of HBO ‘s Real Time With Bill Maher — only days after the two had what he previously referred to as a “great dinner” at the White House.

On Sunday, Trump posted a scathing 1,318-word diatribe on Truth Social blasting Maher as a “complete and total loser” (in all caps).

“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” he began. “He’s got a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO, which was once, long ago, a Network of Quality and Excitement — But that’s all gone. It’s not ‘HOT’ anymore!” (Capitals and uppercasing are all Trump’s.) Trump then turned his ire to producer Chuck LaBella, who’s worked with Maher for years across multiple productions, nothing that LaBella was a “gofer” on Trump’s reality competition show The Apprentice, and also a friend of Trump’s at the time.

“[B]ecause of the success of that show, Number One and Top Rated on many weeks, with the Finale’ [sic] being among the Top Shows of the Year, he was automatically and quickly brought up through the Ranks of NBC, along with everyone else associated with that Historic ‘Happening,'” Trump wrote. “The Success of the Apprentice was so great that everyone partook — It built many careers, and that is a wonderful thing. Some people say it even built my career, because I became President (I would have won without it!). In any event, over the last few years, LaBella would call me nonstop to say, ‘Hello,’ be very nice, and tell me how much Bill Maher ‘loves’ and respects me, and would constantly ask of me, even before I was President, for any form of meeting with Maher and, would I do his show? When I became President, I agreed to meet, after the first one, and the last one, but never agreed to do his show, which he wants me to do, DESPARATELY [sic] — It won’t happen! When I have watched the show, which isn’t often, it always ends with dishonesty, about me at least, but, who cares?”

Trump apparently was upset with Maher over some jokes made on Friday’s installment of Real Time. In his monologue, Maher mocked the president’s approval ratings and recent comments about men’s physiques, while referring to his own recent visit to the White House.

entertainment.title: Jack White Mourns Brother Eddie Gillis, Longtime Manager of Third Man Pressing
entertainment.summary: "The world lost a beautiful soul today,” White wrote of his older brother.
entertainment.body:
Jack White is mourning the death of his older brother, Edward “Eddie” Gillis, who managed Third Man Records’ Detroit vinyl pressing plant.

White shared the news in an Instagram post on Saturday (Oct. 24), writing that Gillis had died that morning “after having fought a tough battle against cancer.” “The world lost a beautiful soul today,” White wrote. “Ed was such a caring, funny and generous person that everybody loved.”

Gillis ran Third Man Pressing for 10 years, overseeing the production of “hundreds of thousands” of records for other artists, White wrote, adding that his brother liked to make small sculptures and flowers from the plant’s vinyl scraps. The facility opened in 2017 in Detroit’s Cass Corridor as part of White’s Third Man Records operation, making White one of the few artists to own his own pressing plant. Before that, Gillis worked as a pastry chef, running kitchens and bake shops for the Ritz-Carlton and Beaumont Hospital. Related Fans Choose LISA's 'Press Play' as This Week's Favorite New Music Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg & Too $hort Electrify Jay-Z30 Tour's Final Stop Olivia Rodrigo's 'You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love' Returns to No. 1 on Billboard 200 Explore Jack White See latest videos, charts and news

White, the youngest of 10 siblings, also credited Gillis with shaping his musical start. “In his youth Eddie was the guitar player in the family when we were all growing up back when I was on drums only, and he was just great at the instrument,” he wrote, recalling that the two played together over the years, once for the Detroit Tigers during spring training in Florida. “He taught me so many wonderful and simple things over the years that I’ll never forget; how to string a guitar, how to fish on the Detroit river, how to drive a stick shift,” White added. “He was an amazing big brother to me and I just hate to see him leave, but I’m glad he is at peace.”

Gillis is survived by his wife, Angie, and their two children, Amelia and Garrett.

White rose to fame as one half of the White Stripes, whose “Seven Nation Army” topped Billboard’s Alternative Airplay chart. As a solo artist, he has sent three albums to No. 1 on the Billboard 200: Blunderbuss (2012), Lazaretto (2014) and Boarding House Reach (2018). Lazaretto also set the record for the biggest vinyl sales week since 1991, a mark it held until 2021.

entertainment.title: Snubs & Surprises at 2026 Caribbean Music Awards: Is ‘Dansa’ Really a Dennery Segment Song?
entertainment.summary: From Lady Lava's domination to head-scratching decisions in newer genre categories, here are the biggest snubs and surprises from the 2026 Caribbean Music Awards.
entertainment.body:
Lady Lava may have dominated the night with four wins, including female soca artist of the year and zess song of the year (“Bob the Builder”), but the fourth annual Caribbean Music Awards certainly avoided clean sweeps.

Co-hosted by Majah Hype and soca star Nailah Blackman at Trinidad & Tobago’s National Academy for the Performing Arts (NAPA) in Port of Spain on Sept. 18, this year’s Caribbean Music Awards marked the first time the ceremony took place in its namesake region. The official broadcast premiered on the official Caribbean Music Awards YouTube page on Oct. 25, delivering a star-studded celebration of the biggest and brightest stars across the contemporary Caribbean music scene.

This year, several new categories were added to the ceremony’s sprawling lineup, including much-needed spotlights of fast-rising genres like bouyon , jab and Dennery segment . Billboard’s Kyle Denis hosted a red carpet livestream on the ground in Trinidad, catching up with a bevy of stars, including eventual winners Kes and Ayetian , as well as the night’s biggest victor, Lady Lava.

Outside of Lava, several other acts took home multiple trophies at this year’s ceremony. Trinidadian brother production duo Full Blown took home three awards, including soca song of the year for “The Greatest Bend Over” (with Yung Bredda) and soca video of the year for “Good Spirits.” They tied as this year’s second-most awarded act alongside pop-dancehall princess Shenseea and French-Haitian konpa singer Joé Dwèt Filé, who swept the konpa and French-Caribbean fields with his smash hit “4 Kampé.” Skillibeng, Kes, V’ghn , Lila Iké , Masicka , Moliy, Ayetian, Silent Addy , and Ravi B also snagged multiple awards.

In addition to over 50 competitive awards, several Caribbean music legends were honored for their timeless contributions to the culture. Billboard Hot 100-charting reggae and dancehall queen Patra earned the Lifetime Achievement Award; Victoire de la Musique winner Calypso Rose received the Elite Calypso Award; konpa giant Alan Cavé scored the Elite Konpa Award; and Belizean-born, Brooklyn-bred hip-hop and political icon Shyne snagged the Global Ambassador Award.

While the ceremony certainly had its heartwarming moments, there were also quite a few head-scratchers. Here are six of the biggest snubs and surprises from the fan-voted 2026 Caribbean Music Awards.

When Klassik Frescobar’s “Dansa” was announced as the winner of Dennery segment song of the year, Saint Lucian Twitter was almost instantly set ablaze. Dennery segment, an offshoot of soca combining elements of kuduro and zouk with Kwéyòl lyrics and dancehall-esque attitude, was developed in Saint Lucia’s Dennery District.

At the city’s Television Centre, it is a behemoth operation. Hundreds of people eat, sleep, and breathe this show for the entirety of its two-month run. Entering the building is not unlike being back at university — the food hall is bustling, people nervously hug one another, and the sound of a live band rehearsing floats through the walls. Unlike university, security here is almost uncomfortably overbearing. A jittery energy — and distinct buzz — percolates. It’s 9 p.m. The countdown to showtime is on, and this team still has something to prove. The Sky spinoff of Lorne Michaels’ long-running NBC sketch show boasted solid viewership numbers in its first installment earlier this year, led by SNL hall-of-famer Tina Fey. Her inaugural episode notched up over 220,000 viewers in Britain, and despite the sharp drop toward the end of the season — Ncuti Gatwa’s closer, up against the Eurovision Song Contest, ended on a series low of 86,420 — critic response was generally fairly warm.

Season two was ushered in by another Hollywood star. Jeff Goldblum, with musical guest CMAT by his side, attracted an overnight audience of 105,000 on Sep. 9. From there, the series again leaned into some of the more niche British names, with Jamie Demetriou, Amelia Dimoldenberg, Danny Dyer and James Norton taking on hosting duties in the next four episodes. (A member of the hair and makeup team names Erivo a standout host on our way to set. She’s proven popular with the cast and crew.)

The cast remains a group of some of the U.K.’s brightest comedy talents: Hammed Animashaun, Al Nash, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Annabel Marlow, Jack Shep, and Emma Sidi all returned for season two. Weekend Update presenters Ania Magliano and Paddy Young saw particular breakout success, and both of them scored sold-out runs for their solo comedy shows at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in August. It’s just the one newcomer this season — Such Brave Girls star Freddie Meredith, who appears in Saturday’s episode as Prince William on The Graham Norton Show . entertainment.title: Peggy King, Singer and ‘George Gobel Show’ Star of Television’s Golden Age, Dies at 96
entertainment.summary: She also recorded several albums for Columbia Records and appeared in Vincente Minnelli’s 'The Bad and the Beautiful.'
entertainment.body:
Peggy King, a television star and singer who rose to prominence in the 1950s, has died. She was 96.

King died Sunday after a long battle with Alzheimer’s disease, her publicist Alan Eicher announced. She had been residing at the Saunders House assisted living facility in Wynnewood, Pennsylvania.

King was best known for her appearances on The George Gobel Show from 1954 to 1957, where Gobel nicknamed her “Pretty Perky Peggy King.” She won an Emmy in 1955 for best female singer for her television work. She also co-hosted the 1958 Emmy Awards. Related Stories Movies Eric Bauza, the Modern Voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Other Iconic Characters, Dies at 46 Movies Ken Atchity, Producer on 'Joe Somebody' and 'The Meg,' Dies at 82

Throughout the 1950s, King appeared on numerous variety programs, including The Bob Hope Show, American Bandstand, The Steve Allen Show, The Jack Benny Program and The Perry Como Show . She also guest-starred on classic television series including Maverick and Dragnet .

King signed a contract with MGM in 1952, leading to a singing cameo in Vincente Minnelli’s film The Bad and the Beautiful , in which she performed “Don’t Blame Me.” She later appeared in the 1955 horror-comedy Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy .

As for as her music career, King performed “Count Your Blessings (Instead of Sheep)” at the 1955 Academy Awards. After Columbia Records executive Mitch Miller signed her to a long-term contract, she released two best-selling albums, Wish Upon a Star and Girl Meets Boy . DownBeat and Billboard named her best new singer for 1955–56.

Composer Arthur Hamilton wrote “Cry Me a River” for King, but Miller refused to let her record it. King later performed the song throughout her career.

Born Feb. 16, 1930, in Greensburg, Pennsylvania, King graduated from Ravenna High School in Ohio. She began singing on radio in Cleveland before joining the bands of Charlie Spivak, Ray Anthony and Ralph Flanagan.
